newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Kangaroos widen boundries of Australian debt.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Kangaroos widen boundries of Australian debt.

text.p: Kangaroos may already be the symbol of Australia, but hopes are now being pinned on them to broaden the horizon of the Australian debt market.

Australian capital markets opened their doors to foreign borrowers with the issue of the "kanagroo" structure in August when Korea Development Bank (KDB) launched a A$150 million fixed rate bond, and two other Korean names have joined the ranks.
Like a samurai in Japan, kangaroos are debt structures issued by foreigners in the Australian domestic market, and other Asian borrowers are already being investigated.

"We do believe we are at the beginning of a new shift in focus of the Australian investor base. And I think that's pretty much as a result of a lack of available investments in Australia for the local market," said Ashley Zimpel, Vice President Department of Debt Markets at Bankers Trust Australia.
BT priced a A$180 million fixed rate kangaroo for Korea Exchange Bank on Tuesday at a spread of 40 basis points over Australian government bonds.
Korea Long Term Credit Bank will have its A$125 million floating rate note kangaroo priced later this week through Commonwealth Bank of Australia, which also lead the KDB bonds.
"When we brought the KDB deal in August that was so successful and so oversubscribed it left the way for other Koreans to follow," said Wayne Hoy, Chief Manager Financial Markets, Commonwealth Bank.

Although Australia's mortgage back securities market has grown and corporate issuance is picking up, albeit slowly, there is still a huge void left by a sharp reduction in debt supply from the Australian Treasury and the state Treasury departments.
The Australian Treasury expects to issue around A$7.0 billion of Treasury bonds in 1996/97, little changed from 1995/96, but down sharply from the A$20 billion seen in 1994/95.

"The Aussie market is going through immense sectoral shift and is happily going to take credits from other markets. An A-minus Korean name and an A-minus Australian name should be absolutely generic in terms of investment," Hoy said.

Australia needs to make this sort of push for foreign business if is to compete within Asia as a financial centre, a point that was clearly made by the Australian Financial Markets Association (AFMA) in its recent annual review.
This showed that turnover in wholesale financial markets had plateaued in the past two years at around A$27 trillion compared with A$25 trillion in 1993/94 and A$21.0 trillion 1992/93.
AFMA chief executive Ken Farrow said that Australian financial markets needed to be much more outward looking and promote itself if it was to compete with the likes of Singapore.

A survey by the Securities Industry Research Centre of Asia-Pacific also showed that Australia's foreign exchange and stock market had lost ground against major centres in Asia and only interest rate derivatives exhibited a competitive position.
However, CBA's Hoy is confident the kangaroo market is well placed to compete for market share within the region. "I think we have the makings of a very healthy market," he said.
Right now it's not the lack of investors that is holding up the growth of the market, its simply borrowers fitting it into their 1996/97 borrowing plans," he added.
